summary: Describes lig, the LISP Internet Groper, a simple tool for querying the LISP mapping database to see which routing locators belong to an endpoint identifier. It is the LISP counterpart of everyday diagnostic tools. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A little tool that asks the big address book where somebody lives right now, so you can check that the book gives the right answer.

questions: how to query the lisp mapping database
how to verify lisp site registration
subtitle: A diagnostic tool for querying the LISP mapping database.

tldr.problem: LISP separates endpoint identifiers (EIDs) from routing locators (RLOCs), and administrators need a way to verify that the mapping database contains correct entries.
tldr.mechanism: The LISP Internet Groper (lig) sends a Map-Request for a destination EID and displays the Map-Reply, showing the EID prefix, locator addresses, and their status.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can diagnose LISP routing problems, verify site registration, and test the Alternative Topology (ALT) infrastructure.

today: RFC 6835 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. The lig tool continues to be used in LISP deployments for diagnostics and verification.

sections.title: What LISP lig Does
sections.content:
The LISP Internet Groper (lig) is a diagnostic tool for the Locator/ID Separation Protocol. LISP splits IP addresses into two parts: Endpoint IDs (EIDs), which are stable addresses used within sites, and Routing Locators (RLOCs), which are topologically correct addresses used on the Internet. A global mapping database stores which EIDs map to which RLOCs.

The lig tool queries this mapping database by sending a Map-Request for a destination EID and displays the Map-Reply it receives. It works on any device that implements LISP, from routers to host systems.
sections.plainLanguage: lig asks the big LISP address book 'where is this person?' and shows you what the book says, so you can check if the answer is right.

sections.title: How lig Works
sections.content:
When you run lig with a destination EID, it sends a Map-Request to a Map-Resolver (or an ALT router if configured). The Map-Resolver either answers directly (if it knows the mapping) or forwards the request through the LISP Alternative Topology to find the authoritative Map-Server. The Map-Server then returns a Map-Reply containing the EID prefix, the locator addresses, and the status (up or down) of each locator.

The output shows the round-trip time and details like priority and weight for each locator, helping operators understand the routing configuration and test connectivity paths.
sections.plainLanguage: lig sends a question to the address book, waits for an answer, and shows you everything the address book said, like 'John is at 10.1.2.3 and also at 10.4.5.6'.

sections.title: Two Main Uses
sections.content:
lig has two primary uses. First, you can query the mapping database for any EID to see where it is currently routed. Second, you can run lig on your own site (using the 'lig self' command) to verify that your site is properly registered in the mapping database. The 'lig self' command sends a Map-Request for one of your site's own EIDs and checks that a Map-Reply comes back, confirming registration.

For IPv6 sites, the 'lig self6' command performs the same check for IPv6 EID prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask 'where does Company X live?' or ask 'do people know where MY company lives?' to make sure your site is in the address book.

sections.title: Implementations and Deployment
sections.content:
Cisco provides a LISP implementation with built-in lig support for both IPv4 and IPv6. There is also a public domain implementation available for any x86-based system, with source code at GitHub. The command syntax varies between implementations but all support specifying the destination EID, an optional source EID, a target Map-Resolver, and the number of retries.

Several web-based monitoring systems use lig on the back-end to automatically poll LISP sites and display their status. These tools help operators monitor the health of the LISP test network.
sections.plainLanguage: Different companies have built their own versions of lig, and some websites automatically ask lig questions all day long to keep a live map of where everything is.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
lig itself does not change the security of LISP; it simply queries the public mapping database. However, because lig provides easy access to mapping information, it is important to protect sensitive mappings. Sites can restrict access to specific mapping entries or place those entries in a private mapping database system that lig cannot reach.

For sensitive sites, the mapping database visibility should be carefully controlled as part of the overall LISP deployment security plan.
sections.plainLanguage: lig is just a tool for asking questions, not dangerous itself, but you should keep your most secret addresses out of the public address book.
